extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history (readers of H. G. Wells' Outline of History)
extracted.subtask_description: A synthetic, popular-history account of the mechanical and industrial revolutions and their social, political, and intellectual consequences across the nineteenth century. Emphasizes technological phases, social change, and the institutional conditions that enabled scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science of Property
rubrics_metrics.description: Working out and applying a Science of Property as a basis for freedom and social justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of five essential constructive tasks that must be achieved before a stable new social and political edifice is possible; credited to the real makers of history in the nineteenth century rather than transient politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science of Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a Science of Currency to ensure and preserve an efficient economic medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the necessary systematic social sciences required to stabilize modern economic life; implies technical, institutional, and policy knowledge to maintain efficient exchange and monetary systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science of Government and Collective Operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing a Science of Government and collective operations so communities can pursue common interests in harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as enabling local and national administration on scales made possible by new transport and communications; a prerequisite for effective modern governance rather than ad hoc rule by statesmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science of World Politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a Science of World Politics to end warfare between races, peoples, and nations and to bring common human interests under common control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as necessary to prevent the 'stark waste and cruelty' of warfare and to manage the international consequences of increased interdependence produced by technology and empire.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-wide System of Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a world-wide system of education to sustain the will and interest of men in their common human adventure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argued as the most important of the fivefold constructive efforts; education is presented both as a moral foundation and as practical necessity for industrial efficiency and democratic participation (examples: night schools, Sunday schools, national schools, spread of evening classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of the Mechanical Revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical revolution progressed in identifiable phases: early steam (pumping engines, Watt), spread of railways and steamships, electrical telegraph and power, then internal-combustion engines and aviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text enumerates examples and dates (Watt, Trevithick, Stephenson's Rocket, first railways from 1830; telegraph from 1835; first undersea cable 1851; electrical light and traction in the 1880s; internal-combustion engines and the aeroplane by 1909) to show cumulative effects on travel time, communication, and administrative scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Mechanical vs Industrial Revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical revolution = development and application of organized science and technology; Industrial revolution = social and financial development (division of labour, factories, concentration of capital).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important conceptual distinction: factories and division of labour could exist independently of steam/coal; the mechanical revolution introduced new material powers that transformed the scale and character of industry and society. The two interact but are root-wise different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture of Scientific Publication and Societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Science progresses by escaping secrecy and personal advantage into publication and a brotherhood of knowledge (e.g., Royal Society, Florentine Society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes institutional and cultural conditions needed for sustained scientific advance: openness, learned societies, and shared publication are shown as roots of the mechanical revolution and prerequisites for continued progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metallurgical Mastery as Prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of metallurgy (rolled iron, sheet iron, steam hammer, Bessemer and open-hearth steelmaking) was a necessary material precondition for large-scale machinery, ships, bridges, and modern construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links specific metallurgical innovations and dates (rolled sheet iron c.1728, rods 1783, Nasmyth's steam hammer 1838, Bessemer 1856, open-hearth 1864) to the possibility of steam engines, locomotives, large ships, and steel-frame buildings; argues scale and kind of new constructions depended on these material advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of Effective Distance and Administrative Scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Transport and communications (railways, steamships, telegraph) dramatically reduced time-distances, enabling administration and unity over far larger areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by numerical examples (Napoleon's pre-rail travel vs post-rail reductions, Liverpool–Manchester 1830, transatlantic crossings reduced to days by 1910) and the implication that political boundaries and administrative organization lagged behind new practical possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Determinants of Technological Adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of machinery depends on relative costs: machinery may be delayed where labour is cheaper; as power gets cheaper and labour dearer, machinery replaces human drudgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why machines did not immediately replace manual gangs everywhere (temporary abundance of cheap labour), and frames the long-term trend of power getting cheaper and labour becoming more expensive as decisive for mechanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular Education as Driver of Political Consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The spread of popular education (night schools, Sunday schools, elementary schools) enabled ordinary people to see, discuss, and organize around the effects of industrialization, fostering class consciousness and mass movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text ties the rise of literacy and education to the visibility of industrial processes, the spread of common reading, and the political mobilization of the working classes (cites German educational investment, Victorian evening classes for shop assistants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class Formation and the Growth of Class Consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial restructuring concentrated property and separated employers and employees, producing a class ('proletariat'/'expropriated') whose shared conditions and education foster a growing sense of solidarity against profit-concentrating classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on Marxian analysis (Marx's prediction of class consciousness), notes how education and mass literacy reduce traditional differences and increase common standards of life, reading, and political identity among workers.
